title: Managing hens through the annual moult
subtitle: Why laying stops, how long it lasts, and what to do to support your birds.
excerpt: Laying hens moult once a year, typically starting in late summer or early autumn as daylight shortens. During the moult, birds stop laying and redirect nutritional resources into feather regrowth. A moult can last 8 to 12 weeks, during which the hen needs higher protein and lower stress than at any other point in the year.
sourceNotes: RSPCA hen welfare guidance, annual moult. Poultry Club of Great Britain, managing the moult. AHDB Poultry, nutrition during moult.

glossaryTerms.definition: The large flight feathers at the outer edge of the wing, numbered 1–10 from the inside out. Primary feather loss sequence indicates how far through the moult a hen is. Replacement of primaries 6–10 indicates the moult is well advanced.

content.text: The moult is not a health problem. It is a physiological event triggered by the shortening day length in late summer. The hen stops laying because growing new feathers requires the same amino acids (methionine and cysteine especially) that go into albumen and yolk. During a moult, your job is to support feather regrowth and reduce stress, not to restore lay.
The moult progresses head-to-tail: head and neck feathers shed first, then breast, body, wing, and tail. Watch the

to judge progress. A hen shedding primaries 7 to 10 is in the final third of her moult. Feathers regrow from pin feathers, which look like dark, waxy tubes emerging from the follicle. Pin feathers are painful if handled; avoid unnecessary handling during this period.

Good-producing hens tend to moult quickly and completely, losing many feathers at once and finishing in 6 to 8 weeks. Poor-producing hens moult slowly, losing only a few feathers at a time over 3 to 4 months. Commercial producers use this as a selection criterion. For small flocks, a slow moult simply means a longer period without eggs from that bird.

Switch to a higher-protein feed (18 to 20% crude protein) during the moult. Some manufacturers produce a specific moult feed or feather conditioner. Others recommend moving to a grower ration temporarily.
Reduce scratch grain during the moult. Scratch is high in carbohydrate and low in protein, and can displace the higher-protein pellets birds need.
Supply clean water at all times. Feather keratin is largely water, and dehydrated birds regrow feathers more slowly.

Lay should resume within two to four weeks of the moult completing, assuming days are artificially extended past 14 hours if you use supplemental lighting. Without lighting, most hens will not resume laying until day length increases naturally in late winter, even if their moult is complete. Second-year hens typically produce 20 to 30% fewer eggs than in their first year.
